strengths: The paper presents a potentially valuable large-scale dataset: 2.7M clips / 7,089 hours, plus a 371K-clip / 1,146-hour HQ subset, with camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and motion instructions. The combination of real dynamic video, spatial annotations, and rich captions targets an important gap between video-generation datasets and 3D reconstruction datasets.

The curation pipeline is reasonably systematic, covering manual source screening, shot segmentation, aesthetic/luminance/OCR/motion filtering, geometric annotation with an enhanced MegaSaM pipeline, SAM2-based dynamic masks, pose-derived motion instructions, and VLM/LLM caption refinement.

The comparison table and dataset statistics indicate that SpatialVID is substantially larger than many existing spatially annotated real-video datasets and covers diverse motion categories and scene types. The HQ sampling strategy attempts to address imbalance in camera motion and semantic categories.
The paper is generally clear about the high-level pipeline and includes useful qualitative examples of annotations, camera descriptions, depth, masks, and dataset distributions.
weaknesses: The central weakness is insufficient validation of annotation correctness. Camera poses and depths are generated by another model pipeline, but the paper provides only qualitative comparisons and distributional statistics, not quantitative pose/depth accuracy on held-out real or synthetic ground truth, failure rates by scene type, calibration errors, or manual audit statistics. For a dataset whose value depends on spatial annotations, this is a material gap.

The claimed superiority of MegaSaM and the modified annotation pipeline is not convincingly supported. Figure 6 is qualitative, and the manuscript does not report numeric accuracy, runtime, success rate, or ablation results for the changes to depth priors, acceleration filtering, or SAM2 dynamic masking.

There is no downstream task evaluation demonstrating that training on SpatialVID improves reconstruction, camera-controlled video generation, captioning, or spatial reasoning. Dataset statistics alone suggest potential usefulness, but they do not establish that the annotations are reliable enough or practically beneficial for model training.

The semantic annotation pipeline relies heavily on Gemini and Qwen, but the paper does not evaluate caption accuracy beyond anecdotal examples and length/statistical analyses. Longer captions and structured tags do not necessarily imply correctness; hallucination, temporal inconsistency, and camera-motion label errors are not quantified.

Reproducibility and release details are under-specified. The dataset is sourced from YouTube, yet the manuscript does not clearly discuss licensing, privacy, copyright constraints, whether videos or only metadata/URLs will be released, access stability, filtering code availability, prompts for VLM/LLM annotation, or exact thresholds for several pose/motion filters.

The comparison with Panda70M is useful but narrow and partly favors the proposed dataset by using filters designed for the authors' camera-motion objective. Broader comparisons against recent spatial-video datasets such as Sekai, DynPose100K, CamVid-30K, and Stereo4D would strengthen the evidence.

Several presentation issues reduce confidence: grammatical errors, inconsistent dataset counts across figures/text, vague phrases such as 'high-quality camera motion,' and some metrics such as TrajTurns/Arc Nums are introduced without enough detail on thresholds or robustness. These are not fatal, but they compound the reproducibility concerns.

strengths: The paper targets an important data gap: large-scale real-world dynamic video with camera pose, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, and motion instructions. If released at the claimed scale of 2.7M clips/7,089 hours, the dataset could be useful for camera-controlled video generation, 3D-aware video modeling, and reconstruction research.

The curation pipeline is reasonably comprehensive in scope, combining manual video sourcing, scene segmentation, visual-quality filters, motion filtering, MegaSaM-based pose/depth estimation, SAM2-based dynamic masks, and LLM/VLM caption refinement.

The manuscript includes comparisons to many related datasets and makes a plausible case that existing resources either lack scale, dynamic real-world content, rich captions, or explicit geometric annotations.

The dataset statistics and qualitative examples indicate some diversity in scene categories, lighting/weather/time attributes, and camera-motion patterns, especially in the proposed SpatialVID-HQ subset.
weaknesses: The evidence for annotation correctness is insufficient. Camera poses and depth are generated by MegaSaM-style pipelines rather than measured ground truth, but the paper provides no quantitative validation against held-out ground-truth datasets, no error rates, no confidence estimates, and only a qualitative visual comparison in Fig. 6. This is a material issue because the main claimed value is geometric annotation quality.

There is no convincing downstream validation. The paper does not train or evaluate a reconstruction, video generation, camera-control, or spatial-reasoning model using SpatialVID, so the claim that the dataset improves model generalization/performance is not supported by experiments.

The comparison with Panda-70M is weak and partly circular: SpatialVID is compared using metrics and filters that were designed for the authors' own curation goals, while other relevant baselines such as Sekai, DynPose100K, CamVid-30K, Stereo4D, or RealEstate10K are not experimentally compared on annotation quality or downstream usefulness.

The data provenance and reproducibility story is under-specified. The dataset is sourced from YouTube, but the paper does not clearly discuss licensing, takedown handling, whether videos or only metadata/annotations will be released, or how future users can reproduce unavailable web videos. Compute costs are listed, but implementation details, prompts, thresholds, sampling rules, and failure handling are not detailed enough for independent reproduction.

Several pipeline choices are arbitrary or insufficiently justified, including aesthetic/luminance/OCR/motion thresholds, temporal smoothing and motion-instruction thresholds, acceleration-based trajectory plausibility checks, and the balancing procedure for SpatialVID-HQ.

The semantic-caption evaluation is mostly descriptive. The paper shows longer or refined captions and one correction example, but does not evaluate factuality, spatial direction accuracy, hallucination rate, or agreement with human annotators. Since LLM/VLM-generated captions are central to the contribution, this leaves a substantial quality gap.

Dynamic masks are claimed via motion probability maps and SAM2 refinement, but there is no quantitative mask evaluation, no analysis of common failures, and no evidence that the masks are accurate enough for training or filtering at scale.

The manuscript contains inconsistencies and presentation issues that reduce confidence: e.g., different reported counts for videos/hours/clips across figures and text, typographical errors, awkward grammar, and some overclaimed language such as 'ground-truth camera motion' despite model-derived annotations.

The paper reads more like a large engineering pipeline report than a fully validated scientific contribution. Scale is the main strength, but the lack of rigorous annotation validation and downstream experiments makes the acceptance case currently unconvincing.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely bottleneck: large-scale real-world video data with spatial annotations for reconstruction, camera-controlled generation, and world modeling. The proposed dataset is substantial, with 2.7M clips, 7,089 hours, and a 1,146-hour HQ subset, which is meaningfully larger than many cited spatial video datasets.

The annotation scope is unusually rich for a dataset paper: camera poses, depth, dynamic masks, structured captions, semantic tags, and serialized motion instructions. This combination is likely useful to multiple communities, including video generation, 3D reconstruction, and embodied/spatial reasoning.

The curation pipeline is fairly comprehensive, combining manual source screening, scene segmentation, quality filtering, pose/depth estimation, dynamic mask refinement, motion instruction derivation, and caption enhancement with pose-aware LLM refinement.

The manuscript gives helpful dataset statistics and comparisons, including motion direction distributions, caption length analyses, semantic tag distributions, and quality/motion comparisons against Panda-70M under the authors' pipeline. These analyses support the claim that the dataset is more motion-rich and spatially focused than generic video corpora.

The paper is generally clear about the motivation and positioning relative to existing datasets. Table 1 makes the contribution easy to contextualize, and the examples in Figures 1 and 14 communicate the intended data format well.
weaknesses: The strongest limitation is the lack of downstream task validation. The paper argues that SpatialVID will improve reconstruction, controllable video generation, and world simulation, but it does not report training or evaluation results showing that models trained with SpatialVID improve on these tasks. For a dataset paper this is not fatal, but it weakens the empirical support for the broader impact claims.

The geometric annotations are pseudo-labels produced by MegaSaM and modified depth estimators, yet the paper sometimes frames them as ground-truth-like spatial supervision. There is no rigorous quantitative validation of pose/depth accuracy on held-out videos with reliable ground truth, nor clear failure-rate/error statistics beyond qualitative comparisons and filtering outcomes.

The comparison to alternative annotation methods in Figure 6 is mostly qualitative and underspecified. The text claims MegaSaM provides the best accuracy/speed tradeoff, but the manuscript does not provide numerical pose/depth metrics, runtime numbers, benchmark details, or enough information to assess the significance of this choice.

Reproducibility of the curation and annotation pipeline is incomplete. Some thresholds are stated, but important details such as manual screening protocol, motion thresholds, smoothing parameters, sampling/balancing rules for SpatialVID-HQ, LLM prompts, and exact acceptance criteria for failed pose estimation are not sufficiently specified for independent reconstruction of the dataset.

The dataset may have selection biases that should be discussed more directly. Querying YouTube with terms such as walk, tour, drone, and drive, and excluding videos dominated by moving foreground objects, likely favors smooth ego-motion and scenic footage while limiting coverage of many genuinely dynamic real-world scenes.

The semantic annotations rely heavily on VLM/LLM-generated captions and tags. The paper shows a plausible correction example, but does not quantify caption accuracy, motion-tag correctness, hallucination rate, or agreement with human judgments, which matters because these annotations are a central contribution.

Presentation has several minor issues, including typos and grammatical errors, some inconsistent terminology, and a few claims that feel overstated relative to the evidence. These are fixable, but they occasionally obscure the technical details.
